newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Executives say Japan will deregulate -- really.
newsitem.headline: Executives say Japan will deregulate -- really.

text.p: Japan will carry out promised reforms, and not just talk about them, because awareness of the need for action had permeated the entire society, Japanese business leaders told an economic forum on Tuesday.

"I think the experience of real economic stalemate we suffered as a result of the bubble economy (bursting) changed the entire social perception about the need of reform and deregulation," Toyoo Gyohten, senior adviser to the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi, said at the World Economic Forum.

"We have been talking about reform and deregulation for years, years, years, and in your view maybe not enough has happened, but in my view...public sentiment is quite different now," he said. The collapse of the bubble economy of inflated stock and property prices in the early 1990s has left Japan with a sluggish economy and wondering if its business and social systems work any more.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) won last month's election on a platform of economic and government reform, and Hashimoto has been quick to set up advisory panels and vow sweeping deregulation of the financial industry.

"I strongly hope Prime Minister Hashimoto is committed to this challenging job of achieving reforms, and we in the business community are giving full support to him," said Masaya Miyoshi, president of Keidanren, Japan's main business lobby.

However, the LDP's history as the master of old-style money politics and back-room deals has led to some scepticism. But the businessmen said the trend toward reform was unstoppable, even if the minority Hashimoto government does not last. "Yes, the LDP has been in the past a kind of cornerstone of the pro-bureaucracy, pro-business, pro-interest-group (system) in Japan," said Hatsuhisa Takashima, executive controller general of Japan Broadcasting Corp (NHK).

But the public had given the LDP an undeniable mandate for slow-but-sure reform, and was even willing to endure some pain, as seen in voters' rejection of an opposition promise to lower the consumption tax which the LDP wants to raise, he said.

Japanese business also needed to mend its ways, for example by re-examining the way Japan's many influential business associations operate, said Yuzaburo Mogi, president and chief executive of Kikkoman Corp.

"It is a fact that some association activities lacked transparency -- accepting retired bureaucrats as directors and serving as the platform for so-called administrative guidance (by the government)," he said.
